human_tolerance.notes: The birds are not shy and will often flit within a few metres of people, especially in forested areas and suburban gardens, picking up flying insects disturbed by human activity such as walking or digging.

phases.name: breeding
phases.note: A seasonal breeder, nesting from August to March in the North Island (the window that applies at Auckland), September to January in the South Island and October to January on the Chatham Islands. Two or more broods are usually raised per season, both sexes build the compact cup nest of moss, bark and fibre bound with spider's web in the forks of trees, the clutch is usually three to four spotted cream eggs, and both adults share the roughly fortnightly incubation. Nest building and incubation of a second brood may begin while the first brood's fledglings are still being fed.

vocalizations.description: An almost metallic cheek, given either as a single sound or, more often, repeated as a chattering. Males also sing a territorial song.

external.note: iNaturalist (P3151), NCBI (P685) and eBird (P3444) ids via Wikidata; GBIF usage key 5231730 matches the GBIF backbone and the ITIS TSN comes from Wikidata P815.

common_names.note: English, French, German and Dutch names from Wikidata P1843. The English name is 'New Zealand Fantail'; 'Grey Fantail' is the second English label on the same property. The Māori name pīriri and pīwakawaka appear in the article rather than on the Wikidata property.

conservation.note: Wikidata P141 records least concern. The article carries no conservation-status statement, so nothing further is claimed.

range.note: Endemic to New Zealand: the article's subspecies list covers the South and Stewart Islands, North Island and Chatham Islands only, and Wikidata P183 records New Zealand as the country it is endemic to.

traits.locomotion_modes.note: 'It flits from perch to perch, sometimes on the ground but mostly on the twigs of a tree', which gives hopping about on the ground and branches; flight is continuous and agile ('almost never still', 'erratic flying behaviour' in the mythology section).

traits.nest_type.note: 'The birds form compact, cup-shaped nests, usually in the forks of trees, made from moss, bark and fibre, and often completed with spider's web.'

traits.size_class.note: From mass_kg: 0.0075 kg falls in the Tiny band.

traits.mass_kg.note: AVONET Mass = 7.53 g. The article gives no weight, and AVONET flags Inference = YES for this species, but the only inferred trait it names is Beak Nares, not mass, so Mass is a measured value. mass_range_kg was left unset rather than guessed, because neither source gives a weight range.

traits.length_m.note: 'It grows to 16 cm in length, of which half is the tail.'

traits.wingspan_m.note: Honest gap. No openly licensed source consulted (English Wikipedia, Wikidata P2050, AVONET) gives a wingspan for the New Zealand fantail. Derived from AVONET's mean wing (chord) length of 74.7 mm at a factor of 2.5, giving 0.19 m; a spread wing's span runs roughly two to three times its chord, so treat this as a range estimate rather than a measurement. AVONET's Kipps distance of 14.9 mm on a 74.7 mm wing (ratio 0.20) indicates a short, broad wing, consistent with the near-constant flutter the article describes.

traits.lifespan_y.note: Honest gap: neither the article, Wikidata nor AVONET states a typical or mean wild lifespan for this species. 3 years is a judgement for a small insectivorous passerine with the high nest failure and predation the article reports (one in four nests abandoned or deserted and just over one in four lost to predation in the urban Wellington study).

traits.diet.note: The article describes the bird as 'looking out for flying insects' and catching 'any small flying insects' disturbed by people, and AVONET independently classifies it as Trophic.Level Carnivore, Trophic.Niche Invertivore. Neither source describes any plant food, so invertebrate is the whole of the recorded diet.

traits.social.note: The article describes a single bird 'flitting from perch to perch' and, separately, 'a flock of fantails' huddling to keep warm in cold temperatures; it never describes a pair bond outside the nest. structure Solitary with group_size 1-6 therefore reflects the solitary-foraging default plus the huddling flock, and the flock size is a judgement because the source gives no number.

traits.activity_pattern.note: 'During waking hours the bird is almost never still.' The huddling behaviour under cold temperatures is a thermoregulatory response, not nocturnality.

traits.defense.note: Authored from the sourced behaviour: the bird's answer to a threat is to flit away to another perch. The article records no threat display, and the predator pressure it does record is on the nest (ship rats and cuckoos), not on adults.

traits.wariness.note: Judgement: 0.12. 'The birds are not shy, and will often flit within a few metres of people, especially in forested areas and suburban gardens.'

habitat.use.note: AVONET Habitat = Woodland and Primary.Lifestyle = Insessorial; the article says the bird perches 'mostly on the twigs of a tree' and 'sometimes on the ground'. arboreal 0.85 / ground 0.15.

habitat.shelter_tag.note: Authored: the nest goes in the forks of trees and the bird works through 'any other convenient object', so shrub_thicket is the closest available shelter tag.

habitat.resources.note: Behaviour section for the aerial insect prey and the perch-to-perch foraging that dominates the day; Breeding section for the cup nest in a fork. No monthly or seasonal weighting was applied because the article describes neither.

habitat.human_tolerance.note: Behaviour section: not shy, flits within a few metres of people, especially in suburban gardens; the Breeding section adds an 81-nest monitoring study in urban Wellington, so nesting in built-up suburbia is normal for this species. Exploiter is the matching affinity. light_max, impervious_max and flight_distance_m are authored judgements.

seasonal.strategy.note: The article describes a resident bird with a seasonal breeding window and no movement or migration at all, and AVONET Migration = 1 (sedentary): ActiveYearRound.

seasonal.phases.note: Breeding section: the North Island August-March window that applies at Auckland (September to January in the South Island, October to January on the Chathams), two or more broods a season, nest construction, clutch size, shared incubation, and the overlap between a second brood and the first brood's fledglings. The phase is restricted to NZ-AUK so a South Island population reads the September-January window instead.

seasonal.life_stages.note: Breeding section: three to four cream eggs, an incubation period of around two weeks, and altricial young; both adults feed. duration_days for the egg is the sourced fortnight. No sourced duration for the juvenile period was found, so it is left unset rather than guessed.

vocalizations.song.note: Behaviour section: "The bird's call is an almost metallic cheek, either as a single sound or (more often) repeated as a chattering." The figure caption identifies a male territorial song, so the call is registered as Song.

look.note: Description section for the plumage: mid to dark grey or grey-brown above, yellowish/orange below, a dark band across the chest below a white throat, white markings over the eye, and white-edged or entirely white outer tail feathers, with a fan-shaped tail shown half the body length; juveniles browner with indistinct markings, and a dark 'black fantail' morph in a few percent of birds. Proportions are authored from AVONET's measurements for this species (culmen 11.8 mm, tarsus 19.4 mm, wing 74.7 mm, Kipps distance 14.9 mm, tail 93.9 mm) read against the biped_winged body plan: a compact, slender bird with a very long fanned tail, comparatively long legs, a short thin bill and a short broad wing. The breast part is coloured to the accent slot so the dark chest band reads, with the belly slot carrying the yellowish-orange underparts.

behavior.note: Authored parameters for the shared perching-songbird program, which fits well: a small perching bird that flushes to a perch, forages by short flights on invertebrates, sings from a perch and builds a cup nest. flee_m 2 reflects the sourced tendency to forage within a few metres of people. Both song and alarm point at the single sourced call, because the article describes no separate alarm call; alarm in this program means flushing to a perch, which is what the sourced behaviour describes. nest_m1/nest_m2 are 8 and 3 for the sourced North Island August-March window, and the shared program's own hard-coded spring months mean nest-building renders in March, April, May and August rather than continuously across that window. song_cooldown_s 12 is a judgement for a bird that calls in single notes or short chatters.
